title: Document a network nobody wrote down
page_title: AP Networking Lab: Document a Network From Its Own Records | Topic 2.2
seo_description: Read a DHCP lease table and an ARP cache to document a small network, and find the one address that tells you something went wrong. AP Networking Topic 2.2.
brief: A small design studio has no network documentation at all. You have been asked to produce some before anything else is changed.
Nobody can tell you what is on the network, but the network can. The router keeps a table of the addresses it has handed out, and the switch keeps a record of which hardware addresses it has seen.
1. Read what the router has leased.
2. Read what the switch has actually seen.
3. One device on this network did not get its address from the router. Find it.
4. Then say what that means, and what you would check first.
An address is not just a label. Some addresses tell you what happened.

questions.prompt: One host is on 169.254.18.44. What does that address tell you?
options: It is a public address, so the device is exposed to the internet
It assigned itself, because no DHCP server answered
It is the router's own management address
It is a loopback address used for testing
questions.explain: EK 2.2.C.3. The whole 169.254.0.0/16 range is APIPA, which a host assigns itself when it asked for a DHCP lease and nothing replied. It is not routable, so the device can talk to nothing beyond its own segment, which is exactly what the user reported.

questions.prompt: Every MAC address in the ARP table starts 3C:22:FB. What does that first half tell you?
options: The subnet the device is on
The manufacturer, because the first 24 bits are the OUI
The order in which the devices joined the network
The port on the switch the device is plugged into
questions.explain: EK 2.2.A.3. A MAC address is 48 bits, and the first 24 are the Organizationally Unique Identifier, assigned to the manufacturer. It is why a rack of identical laptops shares the first half of its addresses, and why the OUI is a useful clue about what an unlabelled device actually is.

questions.prompt: Only one device of the nine shows a 169.254 address. What do you check first?
options: The DHCP server, because it has stopped issuing leases
That device and the port it is connected to
The internet connection, because nothing can reach outside
The subnet mask on every other device
questions.explain: This is the reasoning the address makes possible. If the DHCP server were down, every device asking for a lease would show 169.254, not one of nine. Eight devices hold current leases, so the server is answering. That points at this device or the link between it and the server, which is a completely different repair from restarting a DHCP service.
